blocks.x: Albert Vincent Paul Walters, known as musician Fernandez. How did you get that name? Why did they call you that?

Well, my stepfather raised me and that name just followed Fernandez. And practically all the older musicians know me by the name of Fernandez. I mean my son, Albert's son is a trumpet player and he introduced himself and nobody knows, he's older people, so you've got to explain the name of Fernandez. Then they recognized him, well yeah, I know your father good. And then, Sandra Gordon, a fellow met my son and told him, I don't know Walter. I said, you don't? No, so a fellow buddy told him, a guitar player, he said, well that's Albert Fernandez's son. I said, oh, I used to play jitney dance years ago with your dad.
Well you've got some other nicknames too, Badda, huh?
Badda, yeah. Well Paul gave me that name years ago. Which Paul?
Paul Barber.
Paul gave me that name when he went with Louis Russell. He used to call me Badda.
Now what does that mean?
It's just a name I never could know what it means. He used to advertise me on the placard like that. Kid Badda.
How's it spelled? How would they spell it then?

I don't know, I don't have an idea how to spell it. He used to spell it one way and some people said it was incorrect, you know. And it's spelled another way and some of them spelled it different way, but I never did know the meaning of it.
Well when were you born?
I was born in July of 19, 1905. And where were you born? In New Orleans, Louisiana.
In what section of town?
I was on 2020 Arlene Street. That's in the Tramere. I was Christian at St. Catrion Church. Also made First Communion, confirmed it.
That's over on Tulane Avenue?
Tulane Avenue.
Were any of your family musicals?
Yes, my grandfather was an old time clarinet player. He was a professor in the Al Jays. Alphonse Cobet.
Did he teach clarinet only or teach other music?
No, he taught clarinet only.
Did he play with any band or something like that?
Yeah, he played in band. In fact, I learned in later years that Manuel Mineta came up under him.
Mm-hmm. And when did he die? Did you know him?
Oh, well that's before my dad. I mean, I was quite a kid. I was too young to remember that. Mm-hmm.
Did he have a good age when he died?
I think he died in his 70s.
He's back quite a way. Did anybody else in your family play?

Yeah, I had several cuts and I had James Cobet used to play. He played with a lot of bands around here like Chris Kelly, Charlie Love. I think they made the first trip to Mexico, old Mexico. Oh, yeah. Him, Charlie Love, James Cobet, little dead on banjo. I just remember the lineup. What did he play?
What instrument?
He was an alto and clarinet player.
That's Cobet?
James Cobet. Mm-hmm. And there was another cousin, Reese Cobet. He used to play too. Well, he don't play anymore either.
Is that C-O-B-E-R-T Cobet?
C-O-B-E-R-T-T-E. Cobet. I mean, most of the people around New Orleans, Creole, they call it Cobet. Mm-hmm.
I see. What language did you grow up speaking, by the way? Did you use it? Well, my father and my mother was Creole, you know what I mean?

Practically, we all grew up in Creole. Which they didn't want you to learn that, because they called it, said it was a broken French. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. And just grew up with it. Did anybody around your house sing songs in Creole? Or? Well, my daddy used to, my stepfather. Mm-hmm .
Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm .
Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . and Panuska Fernandez. He'd lived till the age of 109 or 10 like that. In fact, he outlived the old man.
What sort of songs did they sing? Do you remember any of them? Did they sing in Creole?
I couldn't remember this that long. I was quite a youngster. I was in the neighborhood, say about 10, 11 years old.
What instrument did you start on?

Well I started playing piano in house parties. And I went to rehearsal where Kid Howard was playing at a house party on barracks between Ramport and St. Claude. And Johnny Pradoz told Howard, say, well let's make a good piano player. He said try him in another key. So they kept on switching keys and I would follow them. They took my name and address. Well I played several jobs with them. And one day, Henry Allen was looking for a piano player, him and Albert Martin. And I was staying at 1450 St. Claude Street. And they came to my house. And they hired me to play at the Radio Cafe, which is at the corner from here.
Right out on Decatur?
Decatur and Tulip. On that side.
On the uptown side.
And I worked out there with them all about two years, maybe better than two years.
When you started on piano, did you have a piano at home to practice on? Take lessons?

No, I was just taking piano, you know, by going by different people's house like that. And I learned how to play the couple of numbers. And well piano players would skates then, they'd get jammed for parties, they would hire me, you know. And that's how I came out to the light. And after I got with them, well I got to follow music, and in later years, in 1927, 1928 like that, I'd taken to trumpet. Well I learned how to play trumpet a pretty good while. I got in the chamelea band playing piano. And after Wooden Joe got off the trumpet, he had taken sick, I played a couple of jobs in his place. Well Wooden Joe got in bed with the band, and he left. When he left I replaced him on trumpet.
To back up and get some of these different guys' names and instruments. Johnny Prudence was playing with Kit Howard, you say?
That's right.
And what did he play?
He was a string bass player.
And do you remember any of the other guys with Howard?
Well that time we had Big Yank, trombone player. And Yank left to go with Allen. And he got Big Fire in the Yanks' place.
Big?
Big Fire.
Big Fire, who was he? He was a trombone player,
he used to run up and down the coast, they had cut off in them places.
I don't know him. No. Well we'll ask Howard about him.
Oh he had a double of a name around there.
And clarinet, did you have a clarinet or sax? No they had a clarinet,
I think Georgia Lutz was playing with Kit Howard then.
And let's see, who else would be in the band? Drums and banjo I guess maybe.
There was a fellow by the name of Son Thomas was playing banjo with him. He has passed too. I just remember the drummer.
And let's see, after Howard you went with Henry Allen. Went with Henry Allen. That's the young son. The young son, yeah.
Well I played with the Fallen in later years, in the brass band. But I was playing piano then, and I went with Allen during that time.
And who was over there?
With Allen? Yeah. Well they had, I was on piano, Edward Johnson on alto sax, Albert Martin on drum, Big Fire on trombone, and Lil Dad on banjo.
And which Johnson was this on sax? Edward Johnson.
Is that Big Head?
No, the other one, the little bright one. I can't keep those guys straight, there's so many of them.
One is Eddie and one is Edward.
Oh I see. Well Noon is Edward Johnson too, you know. And that's Noon's real name, you know. That really does get confused in there. And then you joined the Camellia you say with Wooden Joe?
I joined the Camellia band, that's right.
Well how was that band set up? Who was the leader and the manager?
A fellow by the name of John Smith.
And what did he play?
He was a banjo player.
And you had a clarinet?
Yeah, I had George Thompson, which everybody knew him by the name of George Stuart.
Oh yeah. You heard Bonk talk about that.
Yeah.
He was a fine clarinet man.
But his real name was what, Thompson?
Thompson. They told me his mother was named Stuart, so everybody called him George Stuart. But of course it might have been a case like me with this Fernandez.
And did you have a trombone player in the band?

Yeah I had a trombone player, a fellow Morris Asano. He's still living, he don't play, he don't care about playing. How old is he? Well Morris should be about 50, in his 50s, in his early 50s I imagine. About 54, 55 like that.
And what kind of music did these bands play? Howard and Henry Allen and the Camelia that was there.

Well they played the numbers that they're playing the dead, the Dixieland numbers like Piano Moore and Dogtown Struthers Ball and Clarinet Marmalet and Fidgeted Feet. The fact that they played all the old numbers that they're using the dead that's in demand.
Were you reading then?

No I wasn't. I learned how to read after I went to play on a Jitney job. Oh I see. I used to buy so much music I just had to learn something. I had fellows in the band to help me and sing along until I learned as much as I did now.
Did you have a teacher on piano at all? Or did you pick it up?
No I didn't have a teacher on piano but the fellow by the name of David John used to teach me when I was working around with him. He used to teach me chords, how to form them and invade them.
Did you have any particular piano player that you used to listen to a lot?

Well I used to like to listen to Clarence Gabriel, Lil Willie, Fat Bichon. Which Lil Willie is that? There was a piano player by the name of Lil Willie. He was a house party piano player. He could play the piano.
Did you see the guy that got killed a couple of Mardi Gras ago? I think it was?
No I think he died a natural death. Willie Forrest, huh?
No, not him. Not Willie Forrest?
No.
Lil Willie.

We used to call him Long-Head Willie. Yeah, Lil Long-Head. He used to play all them house parties. Him, Red Caillou, Udell, Walter Pelliborn. They used to have regular jam sessions like bands they have now on the piano. I was quite a youngster. I used to go around and listen to them. Try to imitate them. Go home and start playing. Try to get what they get on the piano.
Do you still play piano or something?

Well I know the instrument. I'll sit down sometimes and make a few chords but hardly I don't worry with it too much because I don't have it at home. You see if I had one at home probably you know what I mean. I would play at nine then on the job I'd make a few chords.
I have seen you play piano on Burbank Street. I forget who was in the band. Myrtle Jones was singing.
That's right. That's right. The boy didn't know her number and he couldn't play her music so I had to you know fill in.
Oh yeah. When you took up trumpet did somebody help you with that or did you just pick it up?

Well no I went under Chalini when I'd taken up trumpet. I stayed with Chalini about six months and I left him and I went with Manuel Perez. I went with Ole Man Adolf Alexander which we called North Byrne by the name of Taton. I stayed with him about three or four weeks. He was kind of rough. I had to leave him. When you miss your lessons he turned the head with me.
How was Manuel Perez? How did he teach?
Well he was good. He was a good teacher. But Manuel had got sick then. He told me he couldn't continue teaching me because he was sick then. So that made me look for another teacher.
How did he play? Did you hear him very much when you were young?
Oh yeah he was a fine trumpet player. I mean he was a straight man but he was strong. Good leader, fine leader for a brass band.
Did he ever play much in the way of Dixieland numbers or jazz?
Well that's all he could play. He couldn't play nothing else if he wanted to.
I thought maybe in the marches they stuck to the Sousa type marches or something.

Well in the marches sometimes they play marches but I mean the Orleans was always known for that. People like marches. You can mix a few marches but they like the old tradition. You know something they can jump up and holler. And get a kick out of.
When he played the numbers did he play them pretty much the same way every time? Say Panama or? Panama.
Those tunes.
Babyface.
Client and Marmalade. Fidgety Feet. That was the eighth number in the streets. Would he play variations much? No he was a straight man. Straight man.
Straight man. Never varied.

A number he used to play that's Buegel Boy in March. That was the famous number on the street during them days. The same one George Lewis played? Yeah. George learned that from them. That's a good number too. Right? Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. That's a good number. That's a good number. Yeah.
It's a good number. You say he had a big tone loud.
Yeah he had a big tone loud loud. Did he always play carnet or did he? Do you think he switched the trumpet in his last days? Well he in the later days he switched the trumpet.
E flat? Mm-hmm. The little tiny one?
Yeah. What about Woodsville?
How would he compare with Baraz? You say he had a big tone, loud.
Yeah, he had a big tone, loud, loud.
Did he always play cornet or did he? Did you think he switched the trumpet in his last day?
Well, in the later days he switched the trumpet. But when I first met him, he was playing one of those cornet, E-flat cornet.
E-flat?
Mm-hmm. The little tiny one? Yeah.
What about Wooden Hill? How would he compare with Barrage?

Well, I mean, Wooden Hill was a strong trumpet player. But for leading the band, Perez was one of the best. I mean, he used to lead them marches and all. I mean, in other words, he was a musician and all. In other words. But for hardness, for outlasting, I think Wooden Hill was one of the hardest trumpet players they had around Yard.
And what about variations? But Wooden Hill just played straight lead?
No, he'd vary. He'd vary.
He could get off and everything.
Yeah. He'd vary. But he was a hard man.
Did Perez use mute much?
Mute?
Yeah.
Well, yeah, occasionally in the dance hall, like they used to play at the roof garden. Well, I mean, they had the session. The session would use mutes together.
Oh, that's it. Now, what about Wooden Hill? What kind of mutes would he use?
Well, I tell you, Wooden Hill was so strong. Half of the time when he had a mute, now you didn't know he had it. That's the way he got that dance from Wooden Hill.
Well, I know they used to make mutes out of so many different things. I was wondering what different kind of mutes you'd seen.

Well, he had coconut shell. They used to take a coconut and cut it in half and gut out the meat. And they had another little straight mute they used to put in there. Before, wow-wow mutes came in style. They used to wow-wow with that, you know. Put the little mute in there and wow-wow with the half of coconut. Wow-wow, wow-wow, wow-wow, wow-wow.
Is that like a con mute that they had in there?
Yeah.
A pear-shaped?

That's right. Like a little light bulb? Yes. Like a little light bulb. Looked like a little light bulb. Yeah. Then eventually after that they started taking Chris Keller came behind. Well, I mean, he started taking those rubber plungers. And he started making them out of that. Later in the years, I mean, came wow-wow mutes and all the way. You didn't have to use all that. What you had to do is put your hand on it and work it.

Who was in the chameleon band when you came with them? Did they have the same, when you came with them on trumpet, did they have the same line-up? Did they have the same drama, for example? Who was the drama on the bass?
The drama was Alexey Raycart, Raycart's brother.
Oh yeah.

He's passing now too. And the band was John Smith, George Thompson, which is George Stewart. Albert Fernandez Walters on piano. And string bass, Johnny Prudoff. He was playing with that band too. And Mars Asinor on trombone.
And when you came in, you just took Wood and Joe's play, so?
Well, the second time, yeah.
Who did you play with in the meantime, in between?
Well, I played with so many low bands, you know, gigs, they call them. I played with Paul a while. I played with Paul about 13 years.
Paul Barber, I mean. When was that, that you played with Paul, in the 20s or 30s?
Well, it was about in the 30s, say from 36 until about 47.
Was it you who was telling me about playing with a kazoo player in some little trio?

Yeah, I used to play. That's how I started out on piano too. With Danny Barker, and they had a kazoo player by the name of Joe. Well, he did. We used to play that in a little, in a ballroom at Moran Seminole by Rubion. Well, Danny Barker wasn't playing nothing but ukulele then. He was a devil of a ukulele player then. That's how his uncle had sent for him, brought him to New York to learn banjo.
Which uncle was that?
That's Paul Barber in there.
Where were some of the places you played when you started out? What kind of halls? Were they parties or picnics?

Well, I'll tell you, we played at the new hall. The Jean-Germy. The Artesian Hall. The Perseverance. The Economy Hall. The Corporate Hall. St. Catherine Hall. Oh, there's many others that I, you know, just slipped my memory.
Did you ever play many picnics like at Millenburg or anything out there?
Yeah, we used to play picnics at Millenburg, at the Little Evil Camp, the Bombay Lock. There's a lot of others that I, you know what I mean, the members, the names and God of Westman.
You've got a good name.
More roles. We used to play before the police, and the New Orleans had the police band. We used to play the eight day picnic every year. That was from Sunday to Sunday.
In your days when you started, was there anything going on in the Spanish Fort anymore? Was that touring?
Yeah. There was plenty of activities going around there, the Spanish Fort, but I mean, most of the white musicians had, colored musicians, didn't have nothing.
What about West End?

Well, West End, I worked at West End a good while. I worked at the Balloon with a fellow by the name of Munson Hickman, a saxophone player. And we worked at the Bungalow for a while. We left there and went to the C-Plan, and from the C-Plan we went to, well, another fellow used to be a racer around the island, called him Bill Wade. He had a nightclub out there. Well, I worked out there until they completely demolished all the camps. We were one of the last bands out there.
And who were you with out there?
Munson Hickman. Still with him? Uh-huh.
I was wondering about some of the brass bands you played in when you started.
I started out with the Tulane Brass Band, that's Big Landry.
Uh-huh.

Well, they had Landry. Rodgers was the manager of that band. Myself, Kit Howard, Joey Avery, and Isaiah Robertson on trombone, Joey Avery on trombone. And they had a fellow by the name of White, used to play sousaphone. And they had another fellow, Trapp, used to play at mellophone. And Sam Big Tillman playing bass and I used to play alto with the band, alto sax. And Georgia Lewis was in that band also. He used to play that band.
Baratone horn?
Yeah, they had a fellow by the name of Peter White, a West Indian. He used to be baratone.
Oh, yeah, I've heard of those guys. About what year was that when you started the raid?
That was in 1929.
Did they have a bass drummer?
Yeah. Edgar Moses. Edgar Moses. He was the bass drummer. Rodgers was the snare drum man.
How long has Landry been in town? Did you know where he was from or anything?

Landry was from Donisonville. That's his home. Well, he had been in town quite a while, you know, because him and Luz Demere was good friends until he formed this band. Well, I was playing out Millenboy at a nightclub. Well, I had charge of the job. And Rodgers was drumming with me and he told me he used to call me No, he used to call me Dago. He said, Dago, say, how about you come get in the brass band with us? I said, well, I don't know. I said, I don't have no experience in that. I was just, you know, just coming out pretty good. Man, you're doing fine. So he said, why don't you give it a try? So I said, well, all right, I'll give it a try. So I went out with him. That was on a Monday. They had a park out in Suesbury. And they had an egg-dead fare out there. And they played an egg-dead fare out there. And didn't get but half of the money. And when I went back home, my wife said, you'd be the bad snorting the brass band.
There's one thing we always forget to ask people about their school, where they went to school when they were a kid. I don't remember if you told.
Yeah, well, I come up through Catholic school. I used to go to Miss Jeanette until I made my first communion. And after I made first communion, my mother continued with the St. Catherine School.
It's over there on Tulane.
Tulane Avenue.
Where they had the dances near there too. We've got a few more minutes on here. Who were your favorite trumpet players? You mentioned you like Manuel Perez and a few others.
Manuel Perez. Joe, wasn't Joe? Joe Nicklaus.
Did you hear Joe Oliver when you were a kid?
I heard a lot of talk of Joe Oliver. I mean, being young, I just remember, you know.
Very young. But Freddie Kepard, I guess, left town pretty early.
No, I heard Freddie Kepard.
How did you like him?
Oh, he was a fine trumpet player. I also heard Bunk before he...
In the old days.
In the old days, yeah. Before he made his second comeback.
What was he like, Bunk? Bunk? Was he the same as he did later?
I think so. To my idea, he did, yeah.
Who did he play with when you heard him? Was it in the country or right here in the city?

No, in the city. It was a colored nightclub. They called the Entertainers. Anormatwai was working there. He used to go there and wrestle Anormatwai after, you know, he gets off a job here. And everybody would be hollering for him. Bunk, play a number. Play a number, Bunk. But you know he always liked the juice. He had to get his juice voice before he'd get up there. And Anormatwai was another fine trumpet player but he was a different type. He was a sweet type, you know. Sweet, straight, solo.
What would happen when Anormatwai or Perez or that school would have to play a blues? How would they do?

Well Anormatwai could play a blues but they were sweet and soft. It was, you know, more people used to call him a Paula trumpet player. But he could play sweet and soft. He wasn't a flashy trumpet player.
Would he play variations?
Yeah, he would play variations.
Now what would Perez do if he had to play a blues?
Well, Perez would play a straight out blues. Just straight out. There was nothing extra to it. I mean, whatever he played is just like a person who read a poem, you know. It was just straight out.
Would he pick a number like, say, St. Louis Blues or would he just make the blues in B-flat or just anything like that?

Well, B-flat blues or St. Louis Blues. Do you know what I mean? He wouldn't put nothing extra to it. No more than what it'd go. Of course, the average trumpet player or musician, whenever they play a number like that and they would be too far in between, you know, slack in between, they always make some kind of variation to fill in. But he wouldn't. It would be up to somebody else in the band to make that.
Did you hear Buddy Petit much?
Oh, I played with Buddy.
Piano.

Yeah, I played piano with Buddy. Buddy was one of the finest trumpet players. Now, he wasn't strong and powerful, but I mean, he had so much execution. I mean, to my, Buddy, Buddy had the time at the execution that they're using today. I think he's just that far ahead of time. I'd say, I'd put about 40 years ahead of time.
In what ways was his execution good?
In diminishing and chords. Diminishing. That's what they're using today. That's what Buddy made 40 years ago.
Did he play high like Armstrong does?
No, he couldn't play high. That was only his trouble. He never did believe in playing high. He'd stay in the staff and make you sick, though. Make you dizzy with the variation he'd make.
Could you hum a typical variation? Do you remember any of them?
Well, I tell you, he used to play so many variations. He used to practically make a whole lot of different. The immediate execution, under control.
Fingering was good.
Fingering, yeah.
Used carnet or trumpet the times you heard him?
Well, the time I heard him, he had a B-flat trumpet. He was a very fine trumpet player.
What about Kid Rene? How did he compare?

He was a trumpet player on a different type. He had a swell, round tone and clean, clean, clean. I mean, him and Louis Armstrong were about the only two I know on that tone type. It's just a tone. I mean, I heard a lot of trumpet players. I mean, they imitate you, you know, close. A shocker. A shocker played more like Rene than anybody I heard yet. He's styling everything.
Is Rene pretty loud or soft?

Yeah, he was loud. He could get out there on the back of the truck doing the advertising days and get on the back on the tailgate of the truck and stand up there. When he hit, he'd see, this is Claire.
I see.
I see, yeah. This is Claire.
What about Chris Kelly?
Well, Chris Kelly, he was more of a blues trumpet player. In fact, he was one of the best blues trumpets to play their head around here.
What about Papa Celestan? Did he rank with the very best in those days? Was he one of the great players?

Well, yeah, Papa did. He shared. But Papa, I mean, was a different type, too. I mean, that's another type of trumpet. Papa was more of a sweet, sweet type. He had numbers he featured, like Josephine, whenever you launch some telephone to me, well, I mean, he used to specialize.
When did you first play with Papa?
Well, I played a lot of jobs off and on with Papa, you know, but I wasn't regular. I got in a band about five months before Papa died. I was appointed, you know.
I think that about covers most of everything. We only got about two seconds left on here. Okay. Let that run once here.

segments.title: How Albert Walters got the name Fernandez and the nickname Badda
segments.summary: He explains that his stepfather's name stuck as Fernandez, and that Paul Barbarin nicknamed him Badda, advertising him as Kid Badda.

segments.title: Birth in 1905 and growing up in the Tremé
segments.summary: Born July 1905 in New Orleans on Arlene Street; baptized and confirmed at St. Catherine church.

segments.title: Musical family: grandfather Alphonse Cobet and cousins
segments.summary: His grandfather was a clarinet teacher; cousins James and Reese Cobet played with Chris Kelly and Charlie Love, including a Mexico trip.

segments.title: Growing up speaking Creole
segments.summary: The family spoke Creole, which was looked down on as broken French; stepfather sang in it.

segments.title: Starting on piano at house parties and joining Henry Allen at the Radio Cafe
segments.summary: He learned piano at house parties, was tried out by Kid Howard's band, then hired by Henry Allen and Albert Martin for two years at the Radio Cafe.

segments.title: Kid Howard's and Henry Allen's band personnel
segments.summary: Walters names the players in Howard's and Allen's bands: Prudence, Big Yank, Big Fire, Edward Johnson, Albert Martin, Lil Dad, with the interviewers sorting out the Johnsons.

segments.title: Joining the Camellia band and the repertoire
segments.summary: He joined John Smith's Camellia band with George Thompson (Stuart) and Morris Asano, playing old Dixieland numbers.

segments.title: Learning to read and piano influences
segments.summary: He learned to read on jitney jobs, was taught chords by David John, and admired house-party pianists like Lil Willie.

segments.title: Trumpet teachers and Manuel Perez as a player
segments.summary: He studied trumpet with Chaligny, Manuel Perez and a rough teacher; he describes Perez as a straight, strong brass-band leader who never varied.

segments.title: Perez versus Wooden Joe, and trumpet mutes
segments.summary: He compares Perez's leading with Wooden Joe's hardness and variation, then describes coconut-shell and plunger mutes.

segments.title: Camellia band lineup on trumpet and years with Paul Barbarin
segments.summary: He lists the Camellia lineup, then recalls about 13 years with Paul Barbarin in the 1930s and a trio with Danny Barker.

segments.title: Dance halls, picnics and West End
segments.summary: He lists halls and picnic grounds, Spanish Fort, and long work at West End with Munson Hickman.

segments.title: Tulane Brass Band under Big Landry
segments.summary: He joined Landry's Tulane Brass Band in 1929, names its members, and tells how Rodgers recruited him.

segments.title: Schooling at St. Catherine
segments.summary: He went to Catholic school and St. Catherine School on Tulane Avenue.

segments.title: Favorite trumpeters: Keppard, Bunk, and sweet versus straight styles
segments.summary: He recalls hearing Oliver talk, Freddie Keppard and Bunk Johnson at the Entertainers, and contrasts sweet players like Metoyer with Perez.

segments.title: Buddy Petit, Kid Rene, Chris Kelly and Papa Celestin
segments.summary: He praises Petit's execution, Rene's round tone, Kelly's blues, and Celestin's sweet style, and says he joined Celestin's band shortly before his death.
